description_full: Radware Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, develops, manufactures, and markets cyber security and application delivery solutions for cloud, on-premises, and software defined data centers. The company operates in two segments, Radware's Core Business and The Hawks' Business. It offers cloud application protection service, cloud WAF, bot manager, API protection, web DDoS protection, client-side protection, threat intelligence, Kubernetes WAAP, and Alteon integrated WAF; cloud DDoS protection service, web DDoS protection defencepro X, cyber controller, AI SOC Xpert, and firewall-as-a-service; and Alteon, linkproof NG, and SSL inspection services. The company serves healthcare, government, online business, SaaS, education, open banking, MSSP solutions, and financial services through independent distributors, which include value added resellers, original equipment manufacturers, and system integrators. It operates in the United States, the Asia Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and internationally. Radware Ltd. was incorporated in 1996 and is headquartered in Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel.

financial_summary: Radware Ltd. is a small-cap technology business with a $1.3B market cap on $302M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at -1% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 82% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $42M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.47× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 15% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.16x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-3.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 29% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 0.98, it moves roughly with the market.
About $9.9M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.7x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2020 crash, 53% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $7.00 (margin of safety -348%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.06 to $8.33 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 66.8 vs 27.4 and EV/EBITDA 63.4 vs 17.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 22% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $41.50 on average, 32% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 1% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 3.93).
It runs a 82% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow, or 6% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.47x.
ROE of 6% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 26.2% of revenue on R&D and 8.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $121.0M (8% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.5, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.9% over 3 years, 3.8% over 5 years and 3.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.15 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.3x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 4%.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 10, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 12.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 14.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 84%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 14 sales over the past year, net $3.8M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.8% (0.8% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 1,228 employees, each generates about $246K of revenue, 0.7x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 4.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $34K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $1.4M (6x revenue per employee).
